blocks.text: To this very kind of magic Plato alludes in these words in book 2 of the Republic: Θρασύμαχος φαίνεται ὑπό σου ὥσπερ ὄφις κηληθῆναι [Thrasymachos phainetai hypo sou hōsper ophis kēlēthēnai]· Thrasymachus seems to have been charmed by you like a serpent. But whoever wants something more explicit should read, at the end of the Mirabilia attributed to Aristotle [ch. 162], the long story of a serpent called sacred, killed by the spells of a Thessalian witch. Of the same kind is the report that the Indian ἐπῳδοὺς [epōdous], charmers, cure the bites of serpents, as Nearchus, the companion of Alexander, relates, and by flute-players, as Theophrastus relates: the former in Strabo, book 15; the latter in Gellius, book 4, chapter 13. And what Antigonus wrote under the son of Lagus, that the Psylli, when struck by asps, suffer nothing, Mirabilia, chapter 19.
Of this enchantment, moreover, there are many kinds. Some were accustomed to enchant serpents by hand and touch. Virgil, Aeneid book 7, line 754:
Who was wont to scatter sleep by song and by hand.
And Atyr, skilled to disarm serpents of their dire poison and by touch to lull the noxious chelydri to sleep. [III, 165] And book 8, line 500:
They say that Anguitia, offspring of Aeetes, first showed baneful herbs, and tamed poisons by touch.

Symmachus, book 7, letter 19: What Colchian or Thessalian would have relieved these injuries by song or by hand? Others drew a circle and applied drugs. Thus Aristotle, or whoever wrote the Mirabilia, relates that a Thessalian woman in the city of Tenos, in order to kill the sacred serpent, κύκλον γράψασαν, καὶ τὰ φάρμακα θεῖσαν, εἰσβῆναι εἰς τὸν κύκλον αὐτὴν καὶ τὸν υἱὸν [kyklon grapsasan, kai ta pharmaka theisan, eisbēnai eis ton kyklon autēn kai ton huion], having drawn a circle and placed drugs in it, entered that circle with her son. And in Lucian's Philopseudes the Chaldaean, to call forth serpents, came into the field in the morning and read seven sacred names from an old book, θείῳ καὶ δαδὶ καταγνίσας τὸν τόπον, περιελθὼν εἰς τρὶς [theiō kai dadi katagnisas ton topon, perielthōn eis tris], having purified the place with sulphur and a torch, walking round it three times. Again, Seneca describes another rite of enchantment in these words in the Medea, Act 4:
And folding the grim rite with her left hand, she summons the plagues, whatever the sand of burning Libya breeds. — — —

Metal plates, also stones, pieces of wood, and so-called talismanic figures were employed for this use. Arnobius, book 2: Against harmful strokes and the poisonous bites of snakes we often seek remedies, and we protect ourselves with plates sold by the Marsi and Psylli. (Others read, I doubt whether better, We protect ourselves with the lips, with the teeth of the Marsi or Psylli.) And the Nubian Geographer (Clime 1, part 3) tells the fable that near the Nigritian city of Cucu there grows a certain wood which they therefore call عود الحية [ʿūd al-ḥayya] serpent's wood, because اذا وضع علي حجر الحية خرجت اليه مسرعة [idhā wuḍiʿa ʿalā juḥr al-ḥayya kharajat ilayhi musriʿa] when it is placed at a serpent's lair, the serpent immediately comes out to it. Indeed, if we believe it, whoever holds this wood in his hand ياخذ من الحيات ما شا بيده من غير ان يدركه [col. 388] شي من الجزع ويجد في نفسه قوة عند اخذها [yākhudh min al-ḥayyāt mā shā bi-yadihi min ghayr an yudrikahu shay min al-jazaʿ wa-yajid fī nafsihi quwwa ʿinda akhdhihā] will take as many serpents as he wishes in his hand, in such a way that meanwhile he is struck by no fear; rather, in catching them he will feel a certain strength within himself. Others, however, report it differently: namely, that if anyone holds this wood in his hand or hangs it from his neck, لم تقربه حية البتة [lam taqrabhu ḥayya al-batta] no serpent at all approaches him. The same author has this about the city of Emesa, Clime 3, part 5: وهي مطلسمة لا يدخلها حية ولا عقرب ومتي ادخلت علي الباب المدينة هلكت علي الحال [wa-hiya muṭalsama lā yadkhuluhā ḥayya wa-lā ʿaqrab wa-matā udkhilat ʿalā al-bāb al-madīna halakat ʿalā al-ḥāl] It is so talismanized) that is, [III, 166] οὕτω τετελειωμένη [houtō teteleiōmenē], furnished with such τελέσμασι [telesmasi], or talismans), that no serpents or scorpions enter it; rather, if they are brought to the gate of the city, they immediately expire. He adds that in a certain vault a stone is set in which the figure of a scorpion is carved, by touching which a person whom a scorpion has stung or bitten is healed. With the same credibility, in Pliny, book 28, chapter 3, Attalus affirms that if anyone on seeing a scorpion says TWO, it is checked and does not dart its stroke. And Alcamus says that اوس [aws] os, or اوسه [awsah] osoh, is كلمة تقال للحية فتنخضع [kalima tuqāl li-l-ḥayya fa-tankhaḍiʿ] a word which, when said to a serpent, makes it lower itself. Is it because it seems to imitate the hissing of a serpent? For thus in the book of Mirabilia the Thessalian witch, in order to call the sacred serpent into her circle, is said μιμεῖσθαι τὴν φωνὴν τοῦ θηρίου [mimeisthai tēn phōnēn tou thēriou], to imitate the voice of the beast. This is expressed in Arabic by one word, صدا [ṣadā]. Namely, صدا [ṣadā] means to imitate a serpent's hissing in charming it, as Echo imitates our voice. For صدي [ṣadā] is the noun for echo, from which noun the verb صدا [ṣadā] is formed.
